explanation: Read the entire cushion story aloud before asking questions. A listener can show understanding by pointing, acting out a movement, or saying a few words. Model returning to the moment Sam moves his cushion instead of guessing from the title. Mira’s actions change across the story: holding her bag, sitting, then joining the sound. These changes give a small but complete event sequence.

Use the supplied folded-paper model as a book, holding its fold on the left with BOOK upright. Name the front cover, pages, title page, and back cover while touching each part. A title names the book; a picture can show something in it. The cushion story tells made-up events; the book-parts text explains a topic. Neither pictures nor an attractive cover tell us whether every statement is real.

Introduce uppercase M with lowercase m, then S with s. Name each letter and say its common sound: /m/ as at the start of moon and /s/ as at the start of sun; avoid adding “uh.” Children hear spoken words before they see letters. Stretch moon and sun orally to hear beginnings, without asking children to decode those untaught spellings. This week’s print work is matching and tracking with adult reading, not independent word reading.

passages.title: The Cushion Circle
passages.text: On her first morning, Mira stopped beside a circle of cushions. Every cushion seemed to have a child on it. She held her little cloth bag against her coat. Sam looked up and slid his cushion sideways. A small space opened beside him. “Your bag can sit behind us,” he said. Mira tucked it against the wall and sat down. The adult opened a book about a moonlit garden. At first Mira only listened. When the story reached a squeaky gate, she made a tiny squeak. Sam smiled. At the next gate, two voices squeaked together.

passages.title: A Book Has Parts
passages.text: A paper book has a front cover and a back cover. The front cover often shows the title, the name of the book. Pages are between the covers. We turn pages gently so they do not tear. A title page is inside; it usually repeats the title. In English, readers begin at the left of a line and move right. After a line, they go to the next line below. Some books tell made-up stories. Other books give information. Both kinds can have pictures. To make our model book, fold one sheet of paper in half; the adult writes BOOK on its front, BOOK inside on its first page, and END on its back.

explanation: Retelling means giving the important events in a useful order. In Tari’s story, the first cushion does not solve the problem; the box under it does. Use gestures for low and high, then revisit the actual attempts. A child need not repeat every sentence to explain the change from a hidden nose to a visible face.

Write ART BOX and MAT large enough to point to. Move one finger under each spoken word, lifting at the space. A word can contain several letters, so counting letters does not count words. Compare the explanatory labels text with Tari’s made-up picnic while preserving each text’s purpose.

Add A/a, called “ay,” with short /a/ as in apple, and T/t, called “tee,” with /t/ as in top. Model the clipped /t/ without a following “uh.” Review M/m and S/s through mixed matching. The adult reads labels; children track print and hear rhymes in spoken words. Sound examples are oral and are not assigned as decodable words.

passages.title: A Seat for the Bear
passages.text: Tari brought a small toy bear to the table. She set it on a tall chair, but its nose slipped below the table edge. “You cannot see our picnic,” she told it. She tried a flat cushion. The bear was still too low. Then Tari found a little box and put the cushion on top. The bear’s nose rose above the edge. Tari set an empty cup beside it. Her brother came in carrying pretend bread. “Who is our guest?” he asked. Tari pointed to the bear. This time she could see its whole face.

passages.title: Names on Places
passages.text: A label is writing that names something. A classroom can have a label on a door and another on a basket. The basket label may tell what belongs inside. A label can use one word or several words. Spaces help show where one printed word ends and the next starts. Here are two labels for an adult to read while pointing: ART BOX and MAT. ART BOX has two words with a space between them. MAT has one word with three letters. These labels are examples, not words a beginning reader must read alone.

explanation: Read the poem as connected events before calling attention to rhymes. Nia catches drips, wipes prints, and notices the sky. A poem may use short lines, rhythm, and matching sounds; not every poem must rhyme. Demonstrate retelling with three gestures rather than asking for memorization of all eight lines.

The classroom-jobs text explains tasks and a sample chart. Point to CRAYONS and BOOKS as the adult reads them, then point to the names. A chart is a way of arranging information. Distinguish something the sample actually says, such as Paz’s job today, from an unsupported claim about all future days.

Add P/p with /p/ in pan and N/n with /n/ in nest, reviewing A/a, T/t, M/m, and S/s. Rhyme depends on sound from the vowel to the end, not on matching first letters. Say lip, sip, and net without showing print; children listen for the shared /ip/. Ask for a produced rhyme as well as recognition, accepting a nonsense word that preserves the ending.

examples.prompt: Adult model: Which event in the poem comes before Nia wipes the floor?

passages.title: The Rainy-Day Rhyme
passages.text:
A poem for the adult to read with a gentle beat:
Nia put a pan below a drip.
A drop fell in with a tiny flip.
She moved her boots beside the door.
Wet little prints ran on the floor.
She found a cloth and wiped them dry.
A patch of blue peeped through the sky.
Nia left the pan where drops could land.
Then waved outside with one small hand.
After the poem, tell children that Nia is a made-up child. The lines describe what she does during a shower of rain, not a set of instructions for fixing a leak.

passages.title: Our Classroom Jobs
passages.text: Some classroom jobs help everyone use the room. A materials helper puts crayons in their basket. A plant helper checks the pot with an adult before watering; a plant does not need a drink at every check. A book helper places books with their covers facing forward so classmates can see them. Helpers can take turns. A job chart names a job and shows whose turn it is. Our sample chart says: CRAYONS—Noor; BOOKS—Paz. The adult reads the chart. The chart names two helpers today; it does not say they must always do those jobs.

explanation: Listen for the object Imani wants, the places she searches, and the final discovery. Finding a pencil does not mean her search is over: the goal is the yellow ribbon. This distinction helps a child retell an event sequence without replacing the main goal with the first interesting object.

The information passage groups baskets, jars, and trays as containers, then gives distinct features. Have the child use the supplied pretend sorting descriptions rather than fetch materials. Compare handle, lid, and flat bottom by gesture. A topic is the whole group under discussion; a feature belongs to a particular example.

Introduce I/i with short /i/ as in itch and F/f with /f/ as in fan. Review earlier letter names and sounds. Syllables are spoken beats, not the number of letters: basket has two beats, bas-ket. Blend separated syllables without adding extra pauses inside a beat. Pronunciations vary; count the child’s natural spoken version and model the local pronunciation rather than penalizing dialect.

passages.title: The Missing Ribbon
passages.text: Imani wanted a ribbon for the handle of her paper basket. She remembered a yellow ribbon in the art tray, but the tray held only paper scraps. She looked beneath the table and found a blue pencil. She looked beside the shelf and found a crumpled scarf. Finally she asked Finn, who was folding paper birds. Finn lifted a sheet of green paper. There lay the yellow ribbon, curled like a sleepy worm. “It was hiding under my wing paper,” he said. Imani tied the ribbon to her basket. She put the pencil in its cup and the scarf on its hook before carrying the basket away.

passages.title: Containers Help Us Carry
passages.text: A container holds things. A basket can carry several objects at once. Its handle gives a hand a place to hold. A jar can hold small things; a lid can cover its opening. A tray has a broad, flat bottom. It can keep materials together while someone works. Containers are not all the same shape. The best choice depends on the things being held and the job. For a classroom pretend sorting game, put paper circles on a tray and a cloth square in a basket. Do not put anything into an unknown jar.

passages.title: The Little Drum
passages.text: Dev wanted a drum for the classroom parade. He tapped a cardboard box with his fingers, but it made a soft sound. His friend Rosa stretched paper tightly across an empty round container while their adult held it steady. Dev tapped again. This sound was louder. He began to march quickly. Rosa, carrying a paper flag, could not keep up. Dev stopped at the door. “Let us make a slower beat,” he said. Tap, wait, tap, wait. They walked down the hallway together. At the end Dev let Rosa try the drum, and he carried the flag.

passages.title: Making a Paper Chain
passages.text: A paper chain begins with paper strips. An adult supplies strips, a glue stick, and a work mat. Curve one strip into a loop and glue its ends together. Put the next strip through the first loop before joining its own ends. Each new loop links to the last one. If a strip is closed before it goes through a loop, it stays separate. Let the glue dry before lifting the chain. A chain can decorate a shelf. The directions describe paper and glue, not heavy links for climbing or holding weight.

passages.title: The Window Shelf
passages.text:
Omar put three objects on the window shelf: a stone, a paper boat, and a tiny knitted hat. “A museum!” said Gia. Omar shook his head. “A shelf of stories. This stone is a mountain. The boat is going to it.” Gia placed the hat beside the stone. “Then a small traveler left a hat here.” They took turns adding one sentence to the traveler’s adventure. When the adult came to close the window, Omar moved the objects to a tray. “The mountain can travel too,” he said. Gia laughed and carried their story shelf to the reading corner.
Their two-line poem: A boat can float; a hat can ride. Our little tale comes right inside.

passages.title: How Our Small Library Works
passages.text: Our classroom library groups books so readers can find them. One basket holds storybooks with made-up characters and events. Another holds information books about real topics. A poem book may use short lines and playful sounds; some poems rhyme and some do not. A cover and title can give clues, but listening inside a book helps us decide what kind it is. After sharing a book, return it to its labeled basket. Our sample labels are STORIES, INFORMATION, and POEMS. The adult reads these words. A child may choose a book to hear even before being able to read it alone.

passages.title: The Bean in the Boot
passages.text: Hana found an old boot beside the garden shed. A bean seed had fallen into the damp soil inside it. Hana did not notice the seed at first. She set the boot on a sunny step because she liked its red buckle. Several days later a green shoot poked over the boot’s edge. “My boot is growing a surprise,” she told Ben. Their adult helped move the little plant into a larger pot. Hana put a smooth stone inside the empty boot. “Now I know exactly what is in here,” she said. Ben peered inside anyway.

passages.title: A Seed Begins
passages.text: A bean seed can grow into a bean plant when conditions are suitable. Water helps the seed begin to change. A root grows down into the soil. A shoot grows upward. Leaves open on the shoot, and the growing plant needs light. These changes take time; a seed does not become a tall plant during one short story. A larger pot can give a growing plant more room. In our paper model, draw a seed first, a seed with a root second, and a small shoot with leaves third. This is a simple growth sequence, not a promise that every planted seed will grow.

passages.title: The Cart at the Gate
passages.text: Luca and Cora were taking a cart of blocks to the porch. At the garden gate, one wheel caught on a small stone. Luca pulled harder, but the cart stayed still. Cora crouched beside the wheel. “Wait,” she said. She lifted the stone away while Luca held the handle. The cart rolled forward. On the porch they built a low tower. Luca put the stone beside it like a tiny mountain. “This part of our building nearly stopped the whole trip,” he said. Cora added a block bridge over the stone, and the mountain became a tunnel.

passages.title: Tools for Moving
passages.text: People use different tools to move things. A cart has wheels and a space for a load. Its handle helps someone pull or guide it. A wheel can roll along a clear path, but an object in its way may stop it. A basket has no wheels; someone carries it by hand. A ramp is a sloping surface that connects a lower place to a higher one. In our pretend plan, a cart goes up a broad ramp to a porch. The ramp helps the wheels reach the higher surface. These descriptions explain tools; an adult chooses and supervises real moving jobs.

passages.title: A Bell for the Box
passages.text: Eli made a delivery box from a carton. He cut a slot with adult help and painted a blue door. Kira wanted to leave him a folded note, but Eli was across the room building a road. She slipped the note through the slot and waited. Eli did not notice. Kira asked their adult for a little bell. She rang it once beside the box. Eli looked up, hurried over, and found the note. He smiled at Kira’s drawing of two friends. They placed the bell beside the carton. Their next delivery made a bright sound before it was opened.

passages.title: Messages Can Travel
passages.text: A message carries something one person wants another person to know. Spoken words can carry a message when someone listens. A drawing can carry a message too. A written note uses words, and a reader needs to know those words or have help reading them. A signal can tell someone to pay attention. In our classroom example, one tap on a small bell means “a message is waiting.” That bell signal does not tell all the words or show the drawing inside the note. People must agree on a signal’s meaning; the same sound can mean different things in different places.

explanation: Retell the spill without turning it into blame. The paper nudges the cup while Una slides it; the text does not say she deliberately pours water. Then the children divide the repair tasks. Ask what each does and what the new tray changes, using stated actions before judging motives.

The information selection contrasts absorbing water with holding water on a surface. Use the two supplied observations rather than require a real experiment. passages.title: The Cup That Tipped
passages.text: Jules carried a cup of water to the painting table. Una slid a large sheet of paper toward him, and the paper nudged the cup. It tipped. A small river ran across the table. Jules lifted the paint tray out of the water while Una fetched a cloth. They pressed the cloth onto the puddle instead of pushing the water over the edge. Their adult brought a shallow tray for the cup. Una placed a fresh sheet beside it. “This cup has a parking place now,” Jules said. They painted a river on purpose, leaving the real table dry.

passages.title: Absorb and Hold
passages.text: Some materials soak up water. A cloth can take water into its fibers; we say it absorbs water. A plastic tray usually holds spilled water on its surface instead of soaking it up. A cup holds water inside its sides. These objects can help in different ways during a spill. In our described test, an adult puts a spoonful of water on a cloth and another spoonful on a plastic tray. The cloth becomes wet through part of its thickness. Water stays as a puddle on the tray. These are the observations in this example; a different material would need its own check.

passages.title: The Wide Bridge
passages.text: Wren built a bridge for a toy van using two blocks and a strip of card. The van rolled up to the bridge, but the strip was narrower than its wheels. One wheel slipped off. Vik brought a longer strip. “Longer will reach farther,” Wren said, “but we need wider.” They found a broad piece of card and set it across the blocks. The van crossed safely. Then Vik drove a tiny toy bicycle across too. Wren kept the narrow strip. She made it into a path for a little walking figure, who did not need room for two wheels.

passages.title: A Bridge Has a Job
passages.text: A bridge carries a path across a gap. In a classroom model, two blocks can be the supports and a card can span the space between them. The card must reach both supports. The path also needs room for what will cross it. A wide toy needs a wider path than a very narrow toy. Length and width answer different questions: length goes along the trip, while width goes across the path. Our model is only for small toys. passages.title: The Snug Shelter
passages.text:
Quinn tucked a toy fox into a shoebox. The box was so large that the fox slid from side to side when Quinn carried it. Quinn added a folded cloth along one wall and a small cushion at the other end. The fox fitted between them. “Now it is snug,” Quinn said. “It fits closely and comfortably.” Max lifted one corner of the cloth like a blanket. Quinn carried the box across the rug. This time the fox stayed in place. Max put a paper moon above the shelter. “A quiet night for a busy fox,” he whispered.

passages.title: Fitting Things Together
passages.text:
A container and its contents can fit in different ways. A loose fit leaves extra room around an object. A snug fit holds it closely without crushing it. Padding is soft material put around an object. In our packing example, an adult puts a wooden block in a box with folded cloth around its sides. The cloth fills some empty space. It does not make the wooden block softer; it cushions the space around it. These words explain our example, not a rule that all objects should be packed tightly.

They put the thick blocks back. Theo painted stars on the lid instead. “It can be special without being taller,” he said. passages.title: The Fluttering Flags
passages.text:
Ravi tied three paper flags to a string on the porch. At first they hung still. Then a breeze slipped through the railings, and the flags fluttered. They moved quickly back and forth. One flag twisted around the string. Ravi reached for it, but the breeze let go and the flag fell straight again. His sister Ada sat below with a sketchbook. “I cannot draw it in one place,” she said. Ravi held the loose end of the string steady while Ada drew the flags in three different positions. “Now your picture looks busy too,” he said.
Words: written for Liminal. Adult picture plan: three flags on one string, each tilted differently.

passages.title: Words for Moving
passages.text:
Different words can describe movement. Slide means move smoothly along a surface. Roll means turn over and over while moving. Flutter means move lightly and quickly back and forth. In our classroom examples, a wooden block slides on a tray, a ball rolls across a mat, and a paper flag flutters in a breeze. These words help a listener picture how things move. A classroom illustrator can draw arrows beside the objects, but the adult must explain what those arrows mean. An arrow is a mark in the drawing; the object does not grow an arrow.

passages.text:
Lena tipped a little basket, and wooden beads scattered across the rug. They spread in different directions. Some rolled beneath a chair; others stopped against a cushion. “We can gather them,” Bo said. He meant bring them together. Lena set the empty basket in the middle of the rug. Bo found the beads near the chair while Lena checked the cushion. They placed each bead into the basket. At last one green bead remained beside Lena’s shoe. She held it up like a prize before dropping it in. This time she carried the basket with both hands.
Words: written for Liminal. Adult picture plan: show beads in several places on the rug and an empty basket at its center.

passages.title: The Drowsy Dragon
passages.text:
In a made-up story, a small dragon tried to guard a basket of peaches. Each time a leaf moved, he opened one eye. By afternoon he was drowsy: his eyelids drooped and his head nodded. His friend Pip offered to watch the basket while he rested. The dragon curled around a soft blanket instead of the fruit. Pip sat beside the peaches and hummed. When the dragon woke, no peaches were missing. A single leaf lay on top of the basket. “You guarded it from the leaf too,” the dragon joked. Pip tucked the leaf behind one ear.
Words: written for Liminal. Adult picture plan: a dragon with drooping eyelids beside a blanket; Pip sits by the peach basket.

passages.title: Rest and Quiet Spaces
passages.text: A quiet space has fewer loud sounds and fewer busy movements than a lively play area. It may help someone rest or look at a book. Drowsy means sleepy, as if you might fall asleep. Rest can mean sitting calmly without sleeping. In our classroom plan, a rug lies in one corner, two cushions sit on it, and a low shelf holds books. The adult draws this plan and labels the rug QUIET SPACE. The label names the area; it cannot make everyone feel sleepy. People may choose quiet activities for different reasons. passages.title: A Gleam in the Mud
passages.text:
Nell saw a gleam beside a muddy path: a small spot of reflected light. She thought she had found a silver coin. She pointed it out to her uncle, who lifted the object with a stick. It was a shiny bottle cap. Nell looked disappointed. Her uncle set it in a rubbish bag. “It still helped us notice something to clear away,” he said. Farther along, sunlight gleamed on a puddle. passages.text:
Asha made a cape from a square of cloth. When she ran around the garden, the cape caught on a low fence. She stopped before the cloth tore. Her cousin held the corner while their adult lifted it gently off the wood. Asha folded the cape over her arm. “A walking hero for now,” she said. passages.title: Give Cloth Room

An adult should free caught cloth gently because pulling hard may tear it. A play space with clear paths gives people and their materials more room. Our information picture plan shows a piece of cloth caught on a wooden corner, with an adult hand lifting the corner of the cloth. The picture shows where it caught; the words explain why gentle handling matters. This is a classroom discussion example, with adults choosing safe activities.

passages.text:
Rose left a note on the kitchen table before she went into the yard with her grandfather. The note said, “We are by the herb pots.” A breeze from the open window lifted one edge. Rose placed a smooth stone on that edge before going out. Her brother came in later and saw the note beside the stone. He joined them near a pot of mint. “The stone was our quiet helper,” Rose said. Grandfather rubbed a mint leaf between his fingers so they could smell it. Rose decided the next note needed a drawing of the pots too.

passages.title: Why Use a Paperweight?
passages.text: A paperweight is an object used to hold paper in place. In this classroom example, a smooth clean stone rests on one edge of a note. The picture plan shows the stone over a blank corner, with the written lines uncovered. A stone covering every word would not fit that purpose. An adult chooses an appropriate object; the text explains a simple example and does not say every paper needs a weight.

passages.title: The Three Small Signs
passages.text:
Mara made three signs for a pretend museum of shells. One said LOOK, one showed an eye, and one showed a hand with a line across it. Her friend Leo paused at the last sign. “Is the hand waving?” he asked. Mara explained that the shells should stay on the table. They added the words PLEASE LEAVE HERE under the hand. Leo nodded and looked closely at a striped shell. Then Mara moved the signs farther apart so each shell had space beside it. “Our signs need space too,” she said.
Adult picture plan: three table signs separated by gaps; the hand sign has a diagonal line and the adult-written words PLEASE LEAVE HERE.

passages.title: A Sign Needs a Clear Message
passages.text: A sign gives a message where people need it. A picture symbol may need explanation if readers do not know its meaning. Words can help, but someone who cannot read those words still needs support. Place a sign near the thing it describes because a faraway sign may leave readers unsure what it refers to. Leave room around each sign so it can be seen separately. Picture plan: draw a table with two objects and a sign beside each. Draw a second table with both signs piled in one corner. The first plan follows the placement advice; the second can make the message less clear.

passages.text:
Jude wanted a pretend tunnel for large wooden marbles. He set a paper tube between two books, but its opening was too narrow for the biggest marble. Lulu held up a wider tube. Jude tried the big marble first, and it rolled through. They raised one end a little and placed a shallow box at the other end. The marbles rolled down into the box instead of across the floor. Lulu drew their tunnel with arrows showing the marbles’ path. Jude added a large dot inside the box. “That is where the trip ends,” he said.

passages.title: Catch the Rolling Objects

The box should be wide enough for the described objects to land inside. In the picture, arrows show the intended path; they are not measured speeds. This text describes a paper plan for discussion, with an adult choosing any real materials.

passages.title: The Quiet Parade
passages.text:
Five children planned a pretend parade beside the reading corner. Bea carried a paper flute, and Mo held a cardboard drum. When they noticed a child listening to a story nearby, they changed their plan. They marched without playing, lifting their knees and waving little flags. The listener looked up and smiled. After the story ended, the adult led the parade to a different room where the group could try their sounds. Bea drew two panels later: silent marching beside the books and noisy marching in the other room. “Same parade, different place,” Mo said.
Adult picture plan: Panel 1 has books, raised knees, and flags without sound marks. Panel 2 has instruments and sound marks in another room.

passages.title: Make Room for Listening
passages.text: People sometimes need different kinds of space for different activities. A read-aloud group needs to hear the reader’s words. A music-play group may want to explore sounds. In our classroom plan, place sound-making play away from the read-aloud because loud nearby sounds can cover the reader’s voice. The recommendation is about hearing, not about one activity being better than another. Picture plan: one box labeled LISTENING shows a book and seated figures; a separate box labeled SOUND PLAY shows instruments. The space between the boxes represents separate activity areas, not a measured distance.

explanation: Read both short stories more than once before comparing. Ada and Ben both wait for a turn, but Ada makes another part of a picture while Ben observes the playground. A comparison needs a detail from each story; saying that both are “nice” is too vague to show their experiences. Children may use two simple drawings to keep the stories separate.

The information pair describes two ways to manage turns: ordered cards and repeated spoken names. Both make the next turn clearer, but their methods and reasons differ. The Liminal writer composed each text; if the adult makes a two-column drawing, that adult is the classroom illustrator. Ask which text supports a detail before combining information.

Begin this review unit by checking letter names in mixed upper/lowercase sets, then add and substitute sounds orally with new examples. The separate controlled passage is an independent attempt only when the correspondences are secure; otherwise read it with support and record that help. passages.title: Waiting for the Paint
passages.text:
Story A. Ada wanted the blue paint, but Rui was using it for a sky. Ada started a brown tree while she waited. When Rui finished, he slid the blue pot toward her. Ada added a small pond beneath her tree. “My picture grew while I waited,” she said. Rui leaned over to see the pond and asked if he could add a tiny paper boat after the paint dried. Ada nodded.
Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Turn Card
passages.text: Information A. A turn card can show whose turn comes next. In this classroom example, a child places a name card beside a shared paint pot. The next card waits behind it. Move the first card away when that turn is finished. The author recommends keeping the cards in order because the order helps people see who is next. A card does not say how long each child will paint. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Waiting for the Slide
passages.text: Story B. Ben waited behind two children at a pretend playground slide. He counted the steps painted on its side, then looked up when the line moved. At his turn he climbed with the adult watching. From the top he could see the whole play yard. He slid down and joined the end of the line again. “This time I will watch the clouds while I wait,” he said. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Spoken Turn List
passages.text: Information B. A group can also tell turns aloud. The adult names the next child and repeats who will follow. This may help when children cannot yet read name cards. The author recommends repeating the next two turns because a child may not hear the first announcement. This system uses spoken names rather than a row of cards. It does not promise that everyone will remember without another reminder. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: We Can Wait
passages.text: I sit on a mat. You sit on a rug. We have a game. I can hide. You can hide.

explanation: Both protagonists search for a missing object, but their clues come from different sources. Lila remembers her own actions; Omar asks Jo, who moved the block. Ask the child to act out each search and name the clue that helps. Finding an object is the shared outcome, while where and how it is found differ.

The information pair turns those kinds of clues into suggestions. A likely place is not a guaranteed location, and a clear question is more informative than an unclear pronoun. Compare the recommendations and cite their distinct reasons. The stories illustrate experiences; they are not evidence that one search method always works best.

Review case pairs B/b, D/d, P/p, Q/q in mixed order and revisit /b/ versus /d/ without rushing. Substitute final and initial phonemes in fresh oral examples, then compare one-letter print changes. Read known frequent words within connected sentences rather than only isolated flashcards. An independent attempt is optional based on observed sound knowledge, with any adult help recorded.

passages.title: The Missing Mitten
passages.text: Story A. Lila could find only one mitten. She remembered taking both off beside the reading rug. She checked the rug, then the cushion beside it. The second mitten was under the cushion. Lila put both into her coat pocket. Before leaving, she pressed the pocket with her hand to feel the soft pair. Her memory of where she had been helped her choose the first places to search. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Looking Where You Were
passages.text: Information A. Remembering your recent places can guide a search. Our example child last used a pencil at the drawing table, so an adult helps check that table first. Looking in a likely place can focus the search because the object may still be near where it was used. This is a useful clue, not a guarantee. If the object is not there, check another place and ask for help. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Missing Red Block
passages.text: Story B. Omar could not find the red block for his tower. He asked his friend Jo, who remembered putting it with the round pieces by mistake. Together they opened that tray and found the block. Omar gave Jo a blue block for the tower’s doorway, and they finished building side by side. Asking someone who had moved the block gave Omar the clue he needed. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Ask a Helper
passages.text: Information B. Another person may remember moving a classroom object. Ask a clear question, such as “Have you seen the red block?” Naming the object helps the listener know what you mean. The author recommends a specific question because “Where is it?” may not tell the listener which thing is missing. A helper can offer a clue even when the object is not in sight. Text written for Liminal.

explanation: The stories share the purpose of making a shaded pretend space, but the covers and later changes differ. Pia adjusts the doll beneath a leaf; Tomas first uses a card held by an adult, then moves the table. Ask the child to compare actions and materials using two quick drawings rather than treating “both shade” as the entire comparison.

The information texts give distinct reasons for checking a cover and moving a model. A leaf’s patch may be too small; an existing shaded area removes the need for someone to hold a cover. Keep the scope explicitly to supplied classroom models. Picture plans can show object positions; the author’s words supply the stated rationale.

Review E/e, F/f, H/h, J/j, K/k, L/l by name, then use sound manipulations with new CVC examples. Revisit known long-vowel patterns without treating final e as universal. Before the controlled passage, explicitly model the adjacent consonants in trade as /t/ then /r/ followed by long a and /d/; blending adjacent known consonants is supported practice, not a new independent prerequisite.

passages.title: Shade for the Doll
passages.text: Story A. Pia set a doll on a sunny patch of the porch. She wanted a shaded pretend resting place. She stood a broad leaf over the doll using two blocks to hold its stem. The leaf covered the doll’s face but left its feet in the light. Pia moved the doll back a little until its whole body rested in the leaf’s shade. Then she sat nearby and drew the leaf like a green roof. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Small Cover
passages.text: Information A. A broad leaf can make a small shaded patch in a pretend model. Where the shade falls depends on the positions of the leaf and the light. In our drawing, the leaf is above a doll and the shaded patch is beneath it. The author recommends checking the patch before placing the doll because the leaf may not cover the whole chosen space. This is a small-model example, not an outdoor shelter for a person. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Shade for the Table
passages.text: Story B. Tomas wanted shade over a pretend picnic table made from a box. He asked an adult to hold a large sheet of card above it. The card shaded the whole little table. Tomas slid two toy plates underneath and invited Pia’s doll to the picnic. When the adult needed to leave, they moved the table into an already shaded corner instead. The picnic continued without anyone holding the card. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Move to an Existing Shade
passages.text: Information B. A model scene can sometimes move into shade already made by another object. In our classroom example, a box table moves beside a tall block that keeps direct lamp light off one corner. The author suggests moving the table because no one then has to hold a separate cover above it. Check that the chosen spot is actually shaded. This text describes a model under a lamp and does not give weather or sun-safety advice. Text written for Liminal.

weeks.title: Sharing by different plans
weeks.objective: Compare two sharing experiences and two explanations of organizing shared tools.

connection.before: Children can compare both materials and changes in two related stories.
connection.after: Compare routes and directions while keeping information from each source separate.

days: Day 1: Read “One Long Brush” aloud twice. Pause for the child to share one noticed detail, then model the first example.
Day 2: Use Worksheet A orally in two short conversations; reread the exact lines that settle a question. Teach this week’s letter/sound or word work in a separate five-minute session.
Day 3: Read “A Tool Tray” aloud. Model how to point to words the adult rereads as evidence; use part of Worksheet B.
Day 4: Finish selected information tasks, then model the foundations example and use Worksheet C with feedback.
Day 5: Revisit both texts, invite a drawing and oral explanation, and retry a missed foundation skill with support. Record listening comprehension separately from print reading.
explanation: Compare sharing experiences with attention to which resources are shared. Emi and Sol trade painting tools, while Nia and Ash each keep a pencil and take turns with a sharpener. Both stories involve working while another child uses something. Do not replace these concrete differences with an unsupported claim that one pair shares better.

Both information authors recommend an agreed location so a tool can be found. A tray organizes two kinds of tools; the sharpener plan concerns short turns with one tool. Use the supplied labels orally and let the child sketch the arrangements. The texts give organization reasons, not operating instructions.

Review O/o, U/u, V/v, W/w and their taught sounds. Work through addition and substitution before showing print, then compare words that differ by one letter. Practice the unusual parts of to, of, you, have, and put in brief phrases. The controlled text uses known short vowels, a-e/i-e, and introduced frequent words; help is still available without turning listening work into a decoding test.

passages.text: Story A. Ivo made a pretend path to his cardboard castle with flat paper stones. The path curved around a cushion mountain. passages.title: A Route Picture

The whole route stays visible while someone follows one part. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Spoken Path
passages.text: Story B. Sana gave a friend directions for a toy bus: “Go past the blue box, turn beside the mat, and stop at the paper shop.” Her friend stopped too soon, before the mat. Sana repeated the middle direction and pointed to the turn. The bus reached the shop. Next time Sana planned to say one direction at a time, waiting while the bus moved. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: Directions One at a Time
passages.text: Information B. Spoken directions tell a route through words. In our pretend route, the adult says “Pass the box,” waits, then says “Turn by the mat,” waits, and finally says “Stop at the shop.” The author recommends pausing because a listener may need time to move before hearing the next step. Unlike a route picture, spoken words are not still visible afterward; a listener can ask to hear them again. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Leaning Tower
passages.text: Story A. Fen stacked narrow blocks until the tower leaned. He took off the top two and made a wider base from four broad blocks. Fen drew his first base and his new base side by side. “I did not just add more,” he told his friend. “I changed the bottom.” His friend circled the wider base in the drawing. passages.title: Check the Base
passages.text: Information A. In this model-building example, a wide base supports a block tower. Our supplied drawing has two towers of the same height: one with a narrow base and one with a broad base. The text asks readers to notice the base difference. passages.title: The Broken Paper Road

passages.title: Check the Join
passages.text: Information B. A join is a place where pieces meet. In our paper-road example, a patch underneath helps hold two strips together. The author recommends testing the join before extending the road because an open join can interrupt the toy’s trip. The supplied picture plan shows two strips meeting above a small rectangular patch. This is a classroom paper model, not a repair plan for a real road. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Last Seat
passages.text:
Before story time, Mina promised to save a place for Dev, who was returning a tray to the art shelf. She set a small cushion beside her own. More children joined the circle. One child asked to use the cushion, and Mina explained that Dev was coming. They moved their cushions a little closer so there was room for another place as well. When Dev arrived, he sat beside Mina and noticed the extra space. “You saved one and made one,” he whispered. During the story, Mina offered to share the edge of her blanket. Dev tucked it over both pairs of knees.
Adult picture plan: a circle of cushions with Mina and Dev side by side and one extra cushion nearby.

passages.title: Making a Place in a Group
passages.text: A group space can change when more people join. In this classroom example, children sit on cushions in a circle. Moving cushions a little closer makes room for another cushion, while an adult checks that everyone still has enough space. passages.title: The Long Paper River
passages.text: Ari and Bell wanted a paper river wide enough for two toy boats. They put blue strips side by side, but the strips drifted apart on the table. Their adult helped tape the backs together. Bell added a green paper bank along one edge. Ari set two boats on the blue river and moved them slowly past a paper tree. When the boats reached the end, Bell wanted the river to continue. They added another joined pair of blue strips. Ari laughed. “Our river can grow one piece at a time.” They folded the finished paper river carefully to save it for tomorrow.

passages.title: Join, Check, Extend
passages.text: A long paper model can be made in sections. First place two paper strips side by side. An adult joins their backs with tape. Turn the section over and check whether the pieces stay together. Then add another joined section if the model needs to be longer. Checking before extending can reveal a loose join while it is easy to reach. In this described example, the first pair makes one wide section and a second pair extends its length. Width and length are different: adding a strip beside a section changes width, while adding a section at an end changes length.

passages.title: The Hidden Door
passages.text:
Jo built a cardboard house for a toy mouse. The front had two blue windows and one green door. The mouse could not get through because the door was only drawn, not cut open. Jo asked an adult to make a small flap along three sides of the green rectangle. The flap swung outward, and the mouse entered. Jo added a paper path to show the way. When a friend looked at the house from the back, she saw no doorway. Jo turned the house around and opened the flap. “This side tells the rest,” Jo said.
Adult picture plans: Front view has two blue windows, green door flap, and paper path. Back view is plain cardboard. Draw both views.

passages.title: Two Views of One Model

A front-view drawing can show the doorway and path. A back-view drawing will not show them even though they still exist. Labels FRONT and BACK help readers know which side they are seeing. The adult reads those labels. Comparing the views can explain an apparent difference without changing the house itself. The picture plans are a front with one door and a plain back; they do not show the rooms inside.

passages.title: The Quiet Knock
passages.text:
Tess heard three quiet taps while she drew beside the window. She thought her friend was at the door and called, “Come in!” No one entered. The taps came again. Tess listened and turned toward the window. A twig was touching the glass whenever the breeze moved it. Her friend arrived later and knocked twice, much more loudly. Tess laughed. “The tree visited first,” she said. She showed her friend the moving twig. Together they drew two sound pictures: a twig beside a window and a hand beside a door.
Adult sketch plan: one panel shows twig touching glass; another shows a hand knocking at a door.

passages.title: Check Where a Sound Comes From
passages.text: When a sound is unclear, listening again can give more information. In this described classroom example, a light tapping comes from a twig touching a window. A listener first thinks the sound is a door knock. Turning toward the window helps locate it. A picture of a twig and window can show the source once it is known. The words explain the earlier mistaken guess and the later check. This example does not mean every tapping sound comes from a twig. If a real sound needs attention, ask the supervising adult rather than investigate an unknown place alone.

passages.title: The Small Lantern
passages.text: Story A. In pretend play, Amira made a lantern from folded yellow paper. It did not shine, so she drew bright lines around it on her picture. Her brother asked whether it could light the room. “Only in our story,” she said. They carried it to a blanket cave and imagined a glowing path. Later Amira wrote the title with adult help: The Paper Light. She kept the lantern beside the drawing so both could tell part of the invented adventure. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Model and Its Picture
passages.text: Information A. A model can represent something without doing every job of the real thing. Our folded-paper lantern stands for a light, but it has no light source. A picture can add drawn rays to show an imagined glow. Those marks communicate an idea; they do not brighten the room. The supplied picture plan shows folded yellow paper with drawn rays on a separate sheet beside it. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Window Light
passages.text: Story B. Eli sat near a window with a book. A cloud passed, and the page grew dim. He moved to the other side of the table, but that did not restore the earlier brightness. After the cloud moved on, light returned to the same page. Eli drew the book twice, once with gray shading and once bright. His aunt wrote his dictated caption: The cloud changed our light. He showed both drawings when he retold what he noticed. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Changing Brightness
passages.text: Information B. Light on a surface can change. In our described window observation, a page appears dimmer while a cloud blocks some sunlight and brighter after the cloud passes. The two supplied picture panels show the same book with different shading. The panels represent an observed change, while the words explain the timing. A shaded drawing itself does not make the real page dim. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Book for the Next Class
passages.text: Story A. The children made a little book for next year’s class. On the first page, Ren drew the reading corner. On the next, Daya drew the art shelf. Their adult wrote the children’s dictated words beneath each picture. Ren wanted to add every toy in the room, but Daya asked, “What would help someone feel ready on a first day?” They added a page showing a child asking for help. Ren drew an empty speech bubble, and the adult wrote, “Please show me.” When the book was finished, the children left it on the front table with its cover facing up. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Welcome Book
passages.text: Information A. A welcome book can show useful places and actions to a new group. Our sample has a front cover titled OUR ROOM, a title page repeating that title, a page about the reading corner, and a page showing how to ask for help. The adult reads each page aloud while pointing left to right. Pictures show locations and actions; words explain their names or messages. A welcome book is one source of help, and a child can also ask an adult. It does not need to list every object in the room. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: The Welcome Walk
passages.text: Story B. Imani showed a visiting child around the classroom. They stopped at the reading rug and the art shelf. The visitor could not remember where the paper belonged, so Imani walked back with her and pointed to its tray. “We can look again,” Imani said. Before leaving, the visitor placed a small drawing on the tray as a reminder. Imani saved it beside the tray label for the next visit. Text written for Liminal.

passages.title: A Welcome Walk Plan
passages.text: Information B. A welcome walk shows places by going to them. In our sample plan, visit the reading rug first and the art shelf second. Pause for a question at each place. If a visitor forgets where something belongs, return and look together. Unlike a book, the walk lets the visitor see the actual classroom locations. A small picture reminder can help later, but it does not replace a person’s chance to ask again. Text written for Liminal.
